unit.name: Discovering Electronics
unit.subtitle: The fundamental building blocks: systems thinking, circuit laws, resistive components, switching, diodes and combinational logic.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students mix up volts, amps and ohms when labelling readings and answers, especially when units are not printed on the question.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Electronics examiner report Summer 2024 Q3 and Summer 2025 Q3

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students cannot sort sub-system blocks into input, processing and output categories, leading to randomised block placement (e.g. inserting a pulse generator where the specification gives no reason for one).
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Electronics examiner report Summer 2024 Q2 and Summer 2025 Q4

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students try to calculate current using the power dissipation in the zener and series resistor, and believe the regulated voltage changes when the supply voltage rises — the whole point of regulation is that it does not.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Electronics examiner report Summer 2024 Q8 and Summer 2025 Q5

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students add a reverse-bias protection diode around any output device, including lamps and resistive loads. The diode is only needed for ELECTROMAGNETIC loads — relays, solenoids and motors.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Electronics examiner report Summer 2025 QER question (Component 1)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students cannot work backwards from required output current to base current to determine whether VIN is sufficient to saturate the transistor.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Electronics examiner report Summer 2023 Q7, Summer 2024 Q7, Summer 2025 Q8

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students do not know that two NAND gates back-to-back cancel out (double inversion), so cannot identify or simplify NAND-only implementations of standard logic.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Electronics examiner report Summer 2023 Q6, Summer 2024 Q4, Summer 2025 Q2

common_misconceptions.misconception: When a NAND gate has one input tied high or has only one connected input, students still treat it as a two-input NAND rather than as a NOT gate.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Electronics examiner report Summer 2025 Q1(b)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students confuse amplitude with peak-to-peak voltage, and give units of ms for amplitude (or V for period). This propagates into a wrong frequency calculation.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Electronics examiner report Summer 2024 Q7 and Summer 2025 Q2

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students cannot apply k (10³) and μ (10⁻⁶) multipliers correctly inside the f = 1.44/(R₁+2R₂)C formula, leading to answers off by factors of 10⁶ or 10⁹.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Electronics examiner report Summer 2024 Q7

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students do not realise each flip-flop stage divides the input clock frequency by 2, so cannot fill in expected frequencies for Q₀ and Q₁ outputs.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Electronics examiner report Summer 2025 Q6

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students miss the reset pulse mid-sequence and either show the counter stopping or continue counting up past the reset.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Electronics examiner report Summer 2024 Q10 and Summer 2025 Q5

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students swap the positions of the resistor and the thermistor (or LDR) in a voltage divider, producing the opposite output-vs-temperature behaviour to what the specification asks for.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Electronics examiner report Summer 2025 Q6

common_misconceptions.misconception: When asked to complete a half-wave rectifier output graph for a sine wave input, students either leave the question blank or invert the wrong half-cycle.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Electronics examiner report Summer 2025 Q7

student_errors_by_question_type.8 marks — Extended Response: Circuit Ana: QER is the most-omitted question on both papers every year. Even when attempted, students focus on the wrong feature of the circuit (e.g. arguing about a protection diode when the question is about whether the transistor can supply enough current). Teach students to first identify which sub-system the question is testing, then which calculation route confirms or refutes whether the design meets the specification. (Eduqas examiner reports 2023, 2024, 2025).
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Convert to NAND-Only Implement: Students leave NAND back-to-back chains without cancelling the double inversion, producing a circuit with redundant gates. Drill the explicit 3-step algorithm: redraw with NAND equivalents → mark all back-to-back NANDs → cancel them. (Eduqas examiner reports 2023 Q6, 2024 Q4, 2025 Q2).
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Calculation: Multi-Step: Students copy printed equations incorrectly even when they are on the facing page of the question. They also forget to subtract the fixed resistance when sizing a variable resistor in a 555 timer circuit. (Eduqas examiner reports 2024 Q2, 2025 Q1, 2025 Q3).
student_errors_by_question_type.3 marks — Read Off Graph or Oscilloscope: Students give amplitude in ms or period in V, then propagate the unit error into a frequency calculation. Always state the time-base and voltage-base of the trace before reading values. (Eduqas examiner reports 2024 Q7, 2025 Q2).

topic_weighting_notes: Component 1 and Component 2 each carry 40% of the qualification (80 marks each). Coverage is balanced; do not over-weight Component 1 just because it is taught first.
Within each component, AO1 + AO2 = 88% of marks (44% each), AO3 = 12%. The AO3 marks come almost entirely from the 8-mark QER question and the 'design this sub-system' parts.

Mathematical content accounts for a minimum of 20% of the whole qualification — six lessons across the build are calculation-heavy (Ohm's law, voltage dividers, MOSFET equation, op-amp gain, 555 timing, current-limiting LED resistors).

Synoptic questions appear on BOTH papers — Component 1 will ask about Component 2 content and vice versa. Plan questions in the later lessons (Component 1 lesson 10, Component 2 lessons 8-10) that lean on the other unit's concepts.

Highest-scoring topics (2025): circuit analysis, sensing circuits, MOSFETs, inverting amplifiers, oscilloscope traces. Lowest-scoring: block-diagram system design, NAND-only implementations, non-inverting amplifiers, D-type two-bit counters, 555 astable. Allocate more practice questions to the low-scoring topics.
current_spec_changes: Specification is unchanged in content from 2017; Version 5 (December 2025) only updated NEA submission logistics (electronic upload from 2026) and entry codes. Subject content in Components 1 and 2 is identical to the version taught from 2017. (Eduqas GCSE Electronics specification version 5)

From Summer 2026 NEA samples are uploaded electronically and moderated online. This does not affect Component 1 or Component 2 revision content but teachers should clearly annotate mark schemes for online moderation. (Eduqas GCSE Electronics examiner report Summer 2025, p.12)
pedagogical_notes: Practical work is intrinsic to this specification — most exam questions sit in a practical context. Where possible, anchor explanations to a concrete circuit on breadboard (LDR sensor light, 555 LED flasher, comparator night-light) rather than abstract symbol arithmetic. (Eduqas Guidance for Teaching p.1, p.4)

EEF cognitive science guidance: 'retrieval practice was described by the EEF cognitive science guidance review as a cheap, easy-to-implement way of recapping material that might strengthen pupils' long term ability to remember key concepts'. Use the per-lesson 5-question knowledge checks to retrieve the equation set (V=IR, P=VI, MOSFET, 555, op-amp gain) repeatedly across the build. (EEF blog: Why bother with retrieval?)

Cognitive load theory: keep intrinsic load at the right level and strip out extraneous load. Electronics questions often combine 3-4 concepts (e.g. voltage divider + comparator + MOSFET + LED resistor in one circuit). Each lesson should isolate ONE new concept, then practice questions can integrate it with previously-taught material. (Structural Learning, cognitive load theory)

Eduqas Guidance for Teaching recommends teaching Component 1 in Year 10 and Component 2 in Year 11, with practical work integrated throughout. Lesson order in this plan follows the spec sequence so a student revising in either year can jump to the right unit. (Eduqas GCSE Electronics Guidance for Teaching p.2)

The Eduqas GCSE Electronics eBook (free on the resources webpage) is the canonical exemplar resource — content agents should mirror its level of depth and worked-example style but never reproduce its specific problems or wording. (Eduqas examiner report 2025 'further support' section)

lessons_in_batch.title: Diodes, Half-Wave Rectification and Zener Voltage Regulation
lessons_in_batch.description: I-V characteristics of silicon diodes, their protection role in inductive circuits, and zener diodes in voltage regulators.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. Three sub-topics in one lesson because individually they are paragraph-sized. The zener regulator misconception is enormous: 2024 Q8 examiner comment says students 'tried to use the Power of the Zener and Resistor to determine current flow' — wrong approach. 2025 Q5: 'effect of increasing the input voltage having no effect on the voltage across the zener diode' — make this counter-intuitive idea the centrepiece. Smoothing and full-wave rectification are EXCLUDED per Guidance for Teaching p.9. The protection diode is ONLY for electromagnetic loads (relays, solenoids, motors) — 2025 examiner comment flags students added it around lamps unnecessarily.

lessons_in_batch.title: Logic Gates, Truth Tables and Boolean Algebra
lessons_in_batch.description: Reading and building truth tables for NOT, AND, OR, NAND and NOR gates, and writing Boolean expressions.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. Eduqas examiner reports show the truth-table -> Boolean -> circuit pipeline is fragile. 2025 Q1(b): students gave NAND output when input B was unconnected (i.e. NAND configured as NOT) — teach the 'tied input' configuration explicitly. Truth tables up to 4 inputs (Guidance p.10). Boolean expressions kept to sum-of-products of up to 3 inputs, e.g. Q = A.B.C + A.B'.C — no simplification required at this stage. Combinations of up to 5 gates can appear.

lessons_in_batch.title: Designing Logic Systems and NAND-Only Implementations
lessons_in_batch.description: Designing circuits from a specification and converting any logic system to NAND gates only.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Fresh build. 2023, 2024 AND 2025 all flag the same weakness: 'candidates do not know the NAND equivalent circuits for standard Logic gates making identification of double inversions impossible'. Build a NAND-equivalents reference card (NOT, AND, OR, NOR) and drill the conversion algorithm: (1) draw original, (2) replace each gate with NAND equivalent, (3) cancel double inversions. Logic ICs are CMOS 4000 series only per Guidance for Teaching p.10.
